h1: Keeping hops cold from the port to your brewery in Indian heat
title: Keeping Hops Cold From Port to Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: How to protect imported hops from heat at sea, at the port and on Indian roads, with practical checks for when the pallets arrive at your brewery.
teaser: Hops can travel half the world cold and then lose their aroma in one afternoon at an Indian port. Here is where the cold chain breaks.
standfirst: Hop aroma fades with heat, oxygen and time. Imported hops spend weeks in transit before they reach an Indian brewery. The riskiest hours are often the last ones. This guide follows the journey and shows where to put your attention.
sections:
Hop aroma comes from volatile oils. Bitterness comes from alpha acids. Both degrade as hops age. Oxidation speeds up sharply as temperature rises, so a few days at 35 °C can do damage that would take months in a freezer.

Oxidised hops lose their fresh character first, then turn flat and hay-like and eventually cheesy. Beer brewed with them tastes dull and can stale faster. Our guide to hop storage and freshness explains the chemistry.

Hop pellets are normally packed in foil bags that are vacuum sealed or flushed with nitrogen, then boxed. The foil keeps out light and oxygen. As long as the bag stays sealed, the main threat is temperature.

Vacuum-packed bags should be firm and tight. A soft, loose bag has lost its seal and let air in. Nitrogen-flushed bags are softer by design, so check them for punctures and tears instead.
At sea and in the air

Sea freight should travel in a refrigerated container, often called a reefer, with the setpoint agreed with your supplier. Air freight is faster, which helps, but cargo can sit on hot tarmac or in an unrefrigerated warehouse at either end.

Ask for a temperature data logger in every shipment. It is a small device placed among the boxes that records temperature through the journey. When the hops arrive, you can download the record and see exactly when and for how long they warmed up. Without one, you are guessing.
At the port, where most damage happens

Once a reefer container reaches an Indian port, it needs to be plugged into power in the yard. Containers can be unplugged for moving, scanning or customs examination. If documents are incomplete, the container can wait for days.

  • Have your customs broker check all documents before the ship arrives.
  • Confirm that the container freight station has reefer plug points and keeps the container plugged in.
  • Ask your broker to request examination in a cool area where possible and to repack quickly.
  • Book the onward refrigerated truck before arrival so the hops do not wait.

For air cargo, arrange collection as soon as the shipment clears and ask whether the terminal has cold storage.
The last leg on Indian roads

Move hops from the port in a refrigerated truck, not an open lorry with a tarpaulin. For small quantities, an insulated van with ice packs can work over short distances, but a long road trip in May without refrigeration will undo everything that went before.

If you buy from a local importer, ask how they store and deliver. A good importer keeps hops in a freezer room and delivers in insulated boxes. Ask to see their cold room once. You will learn a lot from a two-minute visit.

• Download the data logger and look for warm spells.
  • Check that bags are intact and vacuum packs are still tight.
  • Feel the boxes. Hops arriving frozen or cold are fine. Hops arriving warm need a closer look.
  • Open one bag per lot if anything looks wrong and smell it. Fresh hops smell bright and varietal. Stale ones smell flat, grassy or cheesy.
  • Match lot numbers to the certificate of analysis and note the crop year.

Record what you find. If a lot arrives warm, raise it with the supplier straight away with the logger data. Then put the hops straight into a freezer at around minus 18 °C.

Store hops in a dedicated freezer or cold room, not in the beer fridge where the door opens all day. Keep sealed bags sealed until needed. When you open a bag, use what you need, squeeze out the air and reseal it tightly or vacuum seal smaller portions.

Plan purchases so you do not hold a year of stock. Hops are better bought several times a year in sensible quantities than once in bulk and left to age. The impact of warm handling shows up later in beer that tastes tired, as described in our guide to oxidised beer.

Getting this right does not need expensive equipment. It needs someone in the brewery to own the cold chain and check it every time.
faqs: How cold should hops be stored?
Frozen storage at around minus 18 °C is best for keeping aroma. A fridge at 0 to 4 °C is acceptable for short periods.
What is a temperature data logger?
A small device packed with the shipment that records temperature throughout the journey, so you can see if and when the hops warmed up.
How do I know if hops have been damaged by heat?
Check the logger, the bag seal and the smell. Fresh hops smell bright and varietal. Heat-damaged hops smell flat, grassy or cheesy.
